Last night, I watched the movie, "Get Out." It is a horror movie with the plot seemingly distilled from the "microagressions" hypothesis of Critical Race Theory, a theory that brewed among leftist activist academics for the last few decades and is now part of the mainstream political landscape. A microaggression is a small unintended racial offense by members of a dominant race at the expense of a disadvantaged race. One cliché microaggression is of a white person feeling the nappy hair of a black person, without permission. Even just asking permission would likewise be a microaggression. Or a white person saying to a black person, "You are a credit to your race." Or, "You are so articulate." The Disney movie Zootopia contained this element, but Get Out made it a central theme; the microaggressions turn out to be a reflection of the secret intent to abduct black people and use their superior black bodies to host superior white brains! The series of microaggressions observed by the black protagonist, played by Jordan Peele, provokes a justified paranoia that the seemingly-liberal rich white family is really an enterprise of modern slave dealers. When they touch his arm to feel his stereotypical muscles, they are really estimating his market value. He should have listened to his black friend who told him to never visit the parents of a white chick.

I accept the "microaggressions" hypothesis, except I steer it toward another direction. Critical race theorists focus on the senders of microaggressions. But, communication is always composed of at least two people, and, if a message is perceived but the sender did not intend to send it, then making sense of the message requires understanding the psychology of the perceiver more than that of the sender. Microaggressions are the pattern of perceivers interpreting the signals to be more hostile than the senders intend. This follows from a theory within psychology that is already well-established: us-versus-them mentality. And this theory in turn follows from the more general theory of human ancestral tribalism. We are predisposed to tend to DISTRUST members of an outside group, whereas we are more likely to trust members of our own group. To have an irrational level of caution bordering on paranoia when interacting with a rival tribe follows from natural selection. Your ancestors were more likely to die after trusting members of rival tribes too much than after trusting them too little. It doesn't make much sense in the modern world, but the instinct remains. "Get Out" is a fantasy in which that instinct makes sense. This understanding of racial psychology is discouraging, because it means social divisions are likely to persist for as long as the biological divisions remain.
